 1               CROSS REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF JAMES E. SCOTT, III

 3                       I.    INTRODUCTION AND QUALIFICATIONS
 4   Q.      PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME, YOUR BUSINESS, AND THE CAPACITY
 5           IN WHICH YOU APPEAR IN THIS PROCEEDING.
 6   A.      My name is James E. Scott, III. I am the principal of Earth Intelligence LLC, doing
 7           business as EarthIQ. I appear in this proceeding as an expert witness on behalf of
 8           4K Land and Cattle Company.
 9   Q.      ARE YOU THE SAME JAMES E. SCOTT, III THAT FILED DIRECT
10           TESTIMONY IN THIS PROCEEDING ON MAY 13, 2026?
11   A.      Yes.
12   Q.      WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?
13   A.      The purpose of my cross-rebuttal testimony is to respond to statements made by
14           certain intervening parties in this proceeding. Specifically, a number of intervenor
15           witnesses provided testimony in support of Route 894, including Jason E. Buntz on
16           behalf of Colorado River Alliance Intervenors; Brian C. Andrews on behalf of
17           Glenn Hodge and Ryan Hodge, JT Carothers Holdings LLC, MCP 18 LLC, and
18           Schwertner Farms, Inc.; the Direct Testimony of Mark D. Anderson on behalf of
19           Ben E. Keither Company and Jan Yates Boultinghouse Family Trust. My cross-
20           rebuttal testimony demonstrates that these testimonies, while thorough in their
21           recitation of the Applicants’ own data, share the same fundamental deficiencies I
22           identified in my direct testimony: they present no formal methodology, they adopt
23           the Applicants’ constrained analytical framework without question, they rely on
24           nominal quantitative distinctions that do not support a meaningful “best meets”
25           determination, and they fail to address the statutory criteria that the Applicants’
26           record leaves unanalyzed.
27   Q.      ARE YOU SPONSORING ANY EXHIBITS IN CONNECTION WITH
28           YOUR TESTIMONY?
29   A.      Yes.    I am sponsoring Exhibit JS-1, which I will reference throughout my
30           testimony. Each exhibit was prepared by me directly or was prepared by qualified
     Cross Rebuttal Testimony of James E. Scott, III on Behalf of 4K Land and Cattle Company
     Docket No. 59475
                                                                                                Page 2 of 9



 1           professionals. I have reviewed each exhibit and can attest to its accuracy and
 2           relevance.
 3   Q.      WAS THIS TESTIMONY PREPARED BY YOU OR UNDER YOUR
 4           DIRECTION?
 5   A.      Yes.
 6   Q.      IS YOUR TESTIMONY TRUE AND CORRECT TO THE BEST OF YOUR
 7           KNOWLEDGE?
 8   A.      Yes.
 9                             II. CROSS REBUTTAL TESTIMONY
10   Q.      DO THE TESTIMONIES OF MR. BUNTZ AND MR. ANDREWS OFFER
11           INDEPENDENT ROUTING METHODOLOGIES?
12   A.      No. Mr. Buntz, Mr. Andrews, and Mr. Anderson each accept the Applicants’ filed
13           data, study area, and analytical framework as given and then perform what are
14           essentially confirmatory evaluations within that constrained universe. Mr. Buntz
15           states that he reviewed the Environmental Assessment and Alternative Route
16           Analysis prepared by Kimley-Horn and Halff, publicly available information, and
17           online regulatory data sources, and he concludes that “the selection by
18           Oncor/LCRA TSC of Route 894 as the route that best balances the PURA §
19           37.056(c)(4) and PUC SUBST. R. § 25.101(b)(3)(B) criteria is reasonable and well
20           supported by the environmental information presented in the Application.” Direct
21           Testimony of Jason E. Buntz Direct (“Buntz Direct”) at 5-6. Mr. Andrews similarly
22           states: “Based on my analysis, I agree with the Joint Applicants that Route 894 is
23           the route that best addresses the requirements of the PURA and PUC Substantive
24           Rule § 25.101.” Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews (“Andrews Direct”) at 7.
25           Mr. Anderson likewise testifies that his analysis considered “the Joint CCN
26           Application prepared by Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (‘Oncor’) and
27           LCRA Transmission Services Company (‘LCRA TSC’); . . . the Environmental
28           Assessment (‘EA’) prepared by Kimley-Horn and Halff; [and] the Joint Applicants’
29           route evaluation process and selection of Route 894 as the Best Meets route.” Direct
30           Testimony of Mark D. Anderson (“Anderson Direct”) at 3. His conclusion that
31           Route 894 best addresses the requirements of PURA and PUC Substantive Rules is
     Cross Rebuttal Testimony of James E. Scott, III on Behalf of 4K Land and Cattle Company
     Docket No. 59475
                                                                                                Page 3 of 9



 1           therefore no more than a restatement of the Applicants’ own position — not an
 2           independent validation of it. Anderson at 12. None of these witnesses interrogates
 3           whether the Applicants’ analytical approach itself satisfies the statutory mandate.
 4           As I demonstrated in my direct testimony, the Applicants’ record is not built on a
 5           disclosed, reproducible methodology. See generally¸ Direct Testimony of James E.
 6           Scott, III on Behalf of 4K Land and Cattle (“Scott Direct”). The Applicants
 7           themselves admitted in the related Big Hill to Sand Lake docket that “Neither the
 8           Public Utility Regulatory Act (‘PURA’) nor the Commission’s rules require the
 9           type of quantitative suitability modeling described by Mr. Shipp . . .” Id. at 7. This
10           admission reveals that the Applicants’ process rests on binary constraints, not a
11           thoughtful methodology. Mr. Buntz, Mr. Andrews, and Mr. Anderson, by accepting
12           this framework uncritically, inherit its deficiencies. A confirmatory analysis of a
13           flawed process does not cure the flaw, rather it compounds it.
14   Q.      MR.       ANDREWS            DESCRIBES            A      CORRIDOR-BY-CORRIDOR
15           COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS. DOES THIS CONSTITUTE AN
16           INDEPENDENT METHODOLOGY?
17   A.      Mr. Andrews’s corridor analysis is thorough but ultimately redundant. He divides
18           the 122 filed routes into five corridors — Northern (Link U6), Central using Link
19           J12, Central using Link J27, Central using Link J24, and Southern (Link J32) —
20           and compares routes within and across corridors based on cost, habitable structures,
21           and paralleling existing compatible rights-of-way. Andrews Direct at 14. This is a
22           useful organizational exercise, but it does not constitute an independent
23           methodology because the candidate set itself — the 122 routes and their component
24           links — was generated through the very process I have shown to be
25           methodologically deficient. See generally, Scott Direct. Comparing routes within a
26           universe that was not derived from base terrain analysis does not establish that the
27           universe is geographically complete. As I testified in direct testimony, a boundary
28           derived after routes have already been defined cannot establish that the candidate
29           set encompasses all legitimate alternatives. Id. The territory outside the Applicants’
30           study area boundary was excluded before it was analyzed. Mr. Andrews’s
31           comparative analysis, however sophisticated, cannot remedy this foundational gap.
     Cross Rebuttal Testimony of James E. Scott, III on Behalf of 4K Land and Cattle Company
     Docket No. 59475
                                                                                                Page 4 of 9



 1   Q.      MR. BUNTZ TESTIFIES THAT ROUTE 894 “COMPARES FAVORABLY”
 2           TO OTHER FILED ROUTES. DO YOU AGREE?
 3   A.      Mr. Buntz presents Route 894’s metrics in a manner designed to emphasize relative
 4           advantages, but his own data demonstrates the nominal character of the
 5           differentiation. Mr. Buntz acknowledges that the cost range for all 122 routes spans
 6           from $1,636,232,000 to $1,857,768,000, and that Route 894’s estimated cost of
 7           $1,680,919,000 is only $44,687,000 — or 2.7% — more than the least expensive
 8           route. Buntz at 7-8. He also acknowledges that Route 894 is only 9.18 miles longer
 9           than the shortest route. Buntz Direct at 8-9. These narrow margins are precisely my
10           point. When the cost range across 122 routes spans only $221 million — roughly
11           13% of the median — and Route 894 sits 2.7% above the floor, the quantitative
12           basis for declaring any single route the “best” is vanishingly thin.
13           Mr. Buntz notes that Route 894 has 85 habitable structures within 500 feet of its
14           centerline, “only 5 more than Routes 430 and 442, which have the fewest number
15           of habitable structures” at 80. Buntz Direct at 15-16. A difference of five habitable
16           structures across a 223-mile corridor is not a meaningful basis for route
17           differentiation. These margins fall well within the range of estimation uncertainty.
18           As I established through my Centerline Gravity Index analysis, the 122 filed routes
19           exhibit a CGI of only 3.37% and a preferred-route detour ratio of 1.14 times the
20           great circle distance — metrics that demonstrate the candidate set is not genuinely
21           differentiated. See Scott Direct. Mr. Buntz’s testimony, far from rebutting this
22           finding, inadvertently confirms it.
23   Q.      MR.       ANDERSON            INTRODUCES             A      CORRIDOR-AVERAGING
24           ANALYSIS IN EXHIBIT MDA-3. DOES THIS ADVANCE THE CASE FOR
25           ROUTE 894?
26   A.      No. Mr. Anderson’s corridor-averaging methodology, while superficially
27           informative, actually obscures the route-level distinctions that are relevant to the
28           Commission’s determination. By averaging cost, length, and habitable structures
29           across all routes within each corridor, Mr. Anderson masks the significant variation
30           among individual routes within a given corridor. He concludes that “the South J32
31           and North U6 Corridors should be avoided due to their longer lengths, which are
     Cross Rebuttal Testimony of James E. Scott, III on Behalf of 4K Land and Cattle Company
     Docket No. 59475
                                                                                                Page 5 of 9



 1           on average about 6.9 to 9.4 miles longer than the central J24, J27 and J12 corridor
 2           routes” and “their higher costs, which are on average about $46 - $52 million higher
 3           than Route 894.” Anderson Direct at 9. But corridor averages tell the Commission
 4           nothing about the specific performance of individual routes within those corridors.
 5           A corridor that averages higher in cost may nonetheless contain individual routes
 6           that outperform Route 894 on multiple criteria. The Commission’s statutory
 7           obligation under PURA § 37.056(c) is to evaluate routes, not corridors. Mr.
 8           Anderson’s aggregation methodology is thus fundamentally misaligned with the
 9           Commission’s decisional task.
10   Q.      DOES        MR.      ANDERSON’S            TESTIMONY             REGARDING            COST
11           CONTINGENCY UNDERMINE THE COST-BASED DISTINCTIONS
12           RELIED UPON BY THE ROUTE 894 SUPPORTERS?
13   A.      A. Yes — and significantly so. Mr. Anderson acknowledges in Exhibit MDA-4 that
14           the Applicants’ cost estimates include a contingency of “10% to 15%” to account
15           for “unanticipated events or conditions.” Anderson Direct, Exhibit MDA-4. A
16           contingency range of 10–15% applied to Route 894’s $1,680,919,000 estimated
17           cost produces a band of uncertainty between approximately $168 million and $252
18           million. The entire cost range across all 122 filed routes — $221 million — falls
19           within this single contingency band. This means that the cost differences among
20           routes that Mr. Anderson, Mr. Buntz, and Mr. Andrews rely upon to distinguish
21           Route 894 are smaller than the acknowledged margin of estimation uncertainty. Mr.
22           Anderson’s own exhibit thus fatally undermines the cost-based distinctions on
23           which all three witnesses’ recommendations depend. When every route in the
24           candidate set falls within the same contingency envelope, cost ceases to function as
25           a differentiating criterion.
26   Q.      MR. ANDREWS EMPHASIZES THAT NO ROUTE LESS EXPENSIVE
27           THAN ROUTE 894 HAS FEWER HABITABLE STRUCTURES. IS THIS A
28           COMPELLING ARGUMENT?
29   A.      Mr. Andrews’s observation that “all 44 routes less expensive than Route 894 have
30           more habitable structures within 500 feet of their centerlines than Route 894” is
31           offered as a decisive proof of Route 894’s superiority. Andrews Direct at 8.
     Cross Rebuttal Testimony of James E. Scott, III on Behalf of 4K Land and Cattle Company
     Docket No. 59475
                                                                                                Page 6 of 9



 1           However, this framing is misleading for two reasons. First, it treats cost and
 2           habitable structures as the only two criteria of consequence, to the exclusion of the
 3           other nine codified statutory factors and sub-factors that the Applicants left
 4           unaddressed. The Applicants’ record operatively addresses only two of the eleven
 5           codified criteria — cost and engineering constraints — while leaving community
 6           and landowner impact, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values,
 7           and use of natural or cultural features either unweighted, unquantified, or entirely
 8           unanalyzed. See Scott Direct.
 9           Second, Mr. Andrews’s own data reveals that the trade-offs he identifies are
10           marginal. He acknowledges that Routes 898 and 899 — also Link J27 corridor
11           routes — have the same 85 habitable structures within 500 feet as Route 894, and
12           differ in cost by only approximately $910,000 and $2 million, respectively.
13           Andrews Direct at 28-29. For a project with an estimated transmission line cost
14           exceeding $1.68 billion, cost differentials of less than $2 million represent
15           differences of approximately 0.1% — differences that are plainly within the margin
16           of estimation error. Mr. Andrews effectively concedes this point when he states that
17           “the differences among Routes 894, 898, and 899 are confined to a localized portion
18           between Link F1 and Link G73.” Id. If three routes are this closely matched, the
19           claim that Route 894 is distinctively “best” rests on no meaningful quantitative
20           foundation.
21   Q.      DO ANY OF THE ROUTE 894 SUPPORTERS ADDRESS THE ABSENCE
22           OF A VISUAL RESOURCE MANAGEMENT ANALYSIS IN THE
23           APPLICANTS’ RECORD?
24   A.      No. This is perhaps the most consequential omission in the supporting testimonies.
25           Neither Mr. Buntz nor Mr. Andrews addresses the fact that the Applicants filed no
26           Visual Resource Management (“VRM”) analysis for this project. See Scott Direct.
27           The PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C) criterion — historical and aesthetic values — is a
28           statutory requirement. It cannot be satisfied by silence. Visual contrast introduced
29           by 765-kV lattice infrastructure across 223.7 miles of the Texas Hill Country terrain
30           is a measurable impact on the landscape character, the economic base, and the
31           generational patterns of land use that define this region. See Exhibit CR-JS-1.
     Cross Rebuttal Testimony of James E. Scott, III on Behalf of 4K Land and Cattle Company
     Docket No. 59475
                                                                                                Page 7 of 9



 1           Mr. Buntz limits his testimony to the quantitative data presented in the Applicants’
 2           Environmental Assessment tables — data that do not include any VRM scoring.
 3           See generally, Buntz Direct. Mr. Andrews similarly focuses on cost, habitable
 4           structures, and paralleling existing compatible rights-of-way, and does not address
 5           visual impact at all. See generally, Andrew Direct. Mr. Anderson’s testimony is
 6           equally silent on VRM, despite his claim that Route 894 satisfies all applicable
 7           routing criteria. See Anderson Direct at 13. Without a documented VRM analysis,
 8           the Commission has no basis to find that Route 894 avoids areas of natural beauty
 9           to the greatest extent practicable — and no basis to compare it against alternatives
10           that might do so more effectively. The Route 894 supporters’ silence on this point
11           does not fill the gap in the Applicants’ record; it merely replicates it.
12   Q.      BOTH MR. BUNTZ AND MR. ANDREWS EMPHASIZE THAT ROUTE
13           894 DOES NOT USE LINKS J11 OR J26, WHICH PASS WITHIN THE
14           FOREGROUND VISUAL ZONE OF STATE PARKS. IS THIS ARGUMENT
15           WELL-FOUNDED?
16   A.      The avoidance of state park visual zones is a legitimate consideration, but the
17           manner in which Mr. Buntz, Mr. Andrews, nor Mr. Anderson deploy this factor
18           reveals an asymmetry in their analyses. Both witnesses treat the state parks factor
19           as a near-dispositive screen, using it to eliminate entire categories of competing
20           routes from consideration, while simultaneously ignoring the statutory criterion that
21           should govern this analysis: PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(B), which addresses recreational
22           and park areas broadly, and PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C), which addresses historical
23           and aesthetic values.
24           Mr. Andrews devotes particular attention to the five routes (488, 487, 494, 495, and
25           499) that outperform Route 894 on both cost and habitable structures, but then
26           dismisses them because “each of the five routes uses Link J11 to cross the Colorado
27           River, which places approximately 4.25 miles of ROW within the foreground visual
28           zone of Colorado Bend State Park.” Andrews Direct at 25. He concedes that these
29           routes outperform Route 894 “on four additional routing factors, including all three
30           measures of length not parallel to compatible rights-of-way, and areas of high
31           archaeological potential.” Andrews Direct. Id. The irony is apparent: Mr. Andrews
     Cross Rebuttal Testimony of James E. Scott, III on Behalf of 4K Land and Cattle Company
     Docket No. 59475
                                                                                                Page 8 of 9



 1           applies a rigorous visual impact standard to disqualify routes near state parks but
 2           applies no visual impact standard whatsoever to Route 894’s 223-mile traverse of
 3           the Hill Country landscape. If visual impact is important enough to disqualify routes
 4           near Colorado Bend State Park, it is important enough to analyze along the entire
 5           corridor. Yet no such analysis exists in the record, and no Route 894 supporter calls
 6           for one.
 7   Q.      MR. ANDERSON TESTIFIES THAT ROUTE 894 “COMPLIES WITH THE
 8           COMMISSION’S POLICY OF ‘PRUDENT AVOIDANCE.’” IS THIS
 9           CLAIM SUPPORTED BY HIS ANALYSIS?
10   A.      No. Mr. Anderson’s conclusion that Route 894 “best addresses the requirements of
11           PURA and PUC Substantive Rules regarding certification requirements including
12           ‘Prudent Avoidance’“ (Anderson Direct at 13) is entirely conclusory. He offers no
13           analysis of what prudent avoidance requires in the context of a 223-mile, 765-kV
14           transmission line traversing the Texas Hill Country. He does not identify what
15           specific resources, populations, or land uses are being “avoided” by Route 894. He
16           does not compare Route 894’s avoidance performance against any alternative route
17           on any avoidance metric. And he does not reconcile his prudent avoidance claim
18           with the absence of a VRM analysis or any systematic evaluation of the aesthetic,
19           community, and landowner impacts that a prudent avoidance framework would
20           logically require the Applicants to assess. A bare assertion of compliance,
21           unsupported by methodology or comparative data, does not constitute evidence that
22           Route 894 satisfies Commission policy. It is advocacy, not analysis.
23   Q.      DO THE ROUTE 894 SUPPORTERS ADDRESS THE IMPACT OF LINK
24           K51     ON     THE      COMMUNITIES              AND      LANDOWNERS              IN   THE
25           MCCULLOCH COUNTY CORRIDOR?
26   A.      They do not. Route 894 traverses Link K51, which runs through southeast
27           McCulloch County. As Mr. Frederick Bartlett Wulff, Sr. testified in the Direct
28           Testimony of Frederick Bartlett Wulff, Sr. on Behalf of WBCR, PUC Docket No.
29           59475 (“Wulff Direct”), “proposed link K51 would divide our Brady Creek Ranch
30           and have a severe detrimental effect on the value and use of the ranch.” Wulff Direct
31           at 2. Mr. Wulff further testified that his family has been in McCulloch County since
     Cross Rebuttal Testimony of James E. Scott, III on Behalf of 4K Land and Cattle Company
     Docket No. 59475
                                                                                                Page 9 of 9



 1           1875 and that the impact of Link K51 would not be “isolated or temporary, but
 2           structural and enduring.” Wulff Direct at 26.
 3           Mr. Buntz does not address the McCulloch County corridor at all. Mr. Andrews
 4           acknowledges that Route 894 includes Link K51 in its link sequence but provides
5            no analysis of community and landowner impacts along this segment. Mr.
6            Anderson is similarly silent on the McCulloch County corridor, despite his claim
7            that Route 894 satisfies all applicable routing criteria. See Anderson Direct at 13.
 8           The Commission’s routing sub-factor 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(iii) requires
 9           “moderation of impact on the affected community and landowners.” As I testified,
10           the Applicants left this sub-factor unweighted and unaddressed. See generally,
11           Scott Direct. The Route 894 supporters do not cure this deficiency. They offer no
12           evidence that Route 894’s use of Link K51 moderates community and landowner
13           impact; they simply do not discuss it.
14                                        III.    CONCLUSION

15   Q.      DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR CROSS REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?
16   A.      Yes.




     Cross Rebuttal Testimony of James E. Scott, III on Behalf of 4K Land and Cattle Company
     Docket No. 59475

Map of how rugged and varied the land is across the corridor
area. The red parts are places where tall transmission towers
would change what people see most — dramatic terrain that
doesn’t hide infrastructure well.
 EX-10B · HCI — Hydrologic Characterization Index

Map of where the water lives — streams, springs, and
wetlands the corridor would cross. The red parts are
places where building towers and access roads would
hurt the water and the things that depend on it.
 EX-10C · CEF — Critical Ecological Features

Map of the most important habitat for plants and
animals across the corridor. The bright parts are places
where construction would do the most damage to
living systems we can’t easily replace.
 EX-10D · PPX — People, Places, and Experiences

Map of where people are — homes, ranches, and the
places they go to enjoy the land. The bright parts are
where the power line would change what those
people see, hear, and experience every day.
 EX-CMP · Hill Country Remoteness

Map of how dark the night sky still is across the Hill Country, with the green parts being some of the last truly dark skies in Texas. Tall
transmission towers carry warning lights that would push those dark places toward becoming light-polluted.
 PLATE-F · Four-Perspective Convergence

We used four perspectives to find where best to
locate the route, each one using a different set of
priorities (cost, statute, environment, landowners),
and looked at where each one said the line should
go. The math produced two clear corridor options.

II. CROSS REBUTTAL TESTIMONY
DO THE TESTIMONIES OF MR. BUNTZ AND MR. ANDREWS OFFER
INDEPENDENT ROUTING METHODOLOGIES?
No. Mr. Buntz, Mr. Andrews, and Mr. Anderson each accept the Applicants’ filed
data, study area, and analytical framework as given and then perform what are
essentially confirmatory evaluations within that constrained universe. Mr. Buntz
states that he reviewed the Environmental Assessment and Alternative Route
Analysis prepared by Kimley-Horn and Halff, publicly available information, and
online regulatory data sources, and he concludes that “the selection by

Mr. Andrews’s corridor analysis is thorough but ultimately redundant. He divides
the 122 filed routes into five corridors — Northern (Link U6), Central using Link

and compares routes within and across corridors based on cost, habitable structures,

links — was generated through the very process I have shown to be

universe is geographically complete. As I testified in direct testimony, a boundary
derived after routes have already been defined cannot establish that the candidate
set encompasses all legitimate alternatives. /d. The territory outside the Applicants’
study area boundary was excluded before it was analyzed. Mr. Andrews’s

comparative analysis, however sophisticated, cannot remedy this foundational gap.

MR. BUNTZ TESTIFIES THAT ROUTE 894 “COMPARES FAVORABLY”
TO OTHER FILED ROUTES. DO YOU AGREE?

Mr. Buntz presents Route 894’s metrics in a manner designed to emphasize relative
advantages, but his own data demonstrates the nominal character of the
differentiation. Mr. Buntz acknowledges that the cost range for all 122 routes spans
from $1,636,232,000 to $1,857,768,000, and that Route 894’s estimated cost of
$1,680,919,000 is only $44,687,000 — or 2.7% — more than the least expensive
route. Buntz at 7-8. He also acknowledges that Route 894 is only 9.18 miles longer
than the shortest route. Buntz Direct at 8-9. These narrow margins are precisely my
point. When the cost range across 122 routes spans only $221 million — roughly
13% of the median — and Route 894 sits 2.7% above the floor, the quantitative
basis for declaring any single route the “best” is vanishingly thin.

Mr. Buntz notes that Route 894 has 85 habitable structures within 500 feet of its
centerline, “only 5 more than Routes 430 and 442, which have the fewest number
of habitable structures” at 80. Buntz Direct at 15-16. A difference of five habitable
structures across a 223-mile corridor is not a meaningful basis for route
differentiation. These margins fall well within the range of estimation uncertainty.
As Lestablished through my Centerline Gravity Index analysis, the 122 filed routes
exhibit a CGI of only 3.37% and a preferred-route detour ratio of 1.14 times the
great circle distance — metrics that demonstrate the candidate set is not genuinely
differentiated. See Scott Direct. Mr. Buntz’s testimony, far from rebutting this
finding, inadvertently confirms it.

DOES MR. ANDERSON’S TESTIMONY REGARDING COST
CONTINGENCY UNDERMINE THE COST-BASED DISTINCTIONS

A. Yes — and significantly so. Mr. Anderson acknowledges in Exhibit MDA-4 that

contingency range of 10-15% applied to Route 894’s $1,680,919,000 estimated

million. The entire cost range across all 122 filed routes — $221 million — falls
within this single contingency band. This means that the cost differences among

Route 894 are smaller than the acknowledged margin of estimation uncertainty. Mr.
Anderson’s own exhibit thus fatally undermines the cost-based distinctions on
which all three witnesses’ recommendations depend. When every route in the
candidate set falls within the same contingency envelope, cost ceases to function as
a differentiating criterion.
